lesson_title: Conversions, Volume and Surface Area: the Tank, the Oven and the Paint Tin
hook_text: The brochure says the tank holds 5 500 litres. One formula tells you if the supplier is lying.
clip_script: New rainwater tank in the yard: 2,2 metres across, 1,5 metres tall. The brochure promises 5 500 litres. Check it yourself. First trap: 2,2 is the width — the radius is HALF that, 1,1. Use the full width and your answer comes out four times too big, because the radius gets squared. Now the recipe: floor circle times height. Pi times 1,1 squared — that's 3,142 times 1,21, about 3,802 square metres of floor. Stack the water 1,5 high: 5,703 cubic metres. And every cubic metre swallows exactly a thousand litres — so 5 703 litres. Brochure said 5 500. Supplier told the truth. Now the paint. Peel the tank's wall like a label off a tin of beans — it flattens into a rectangle: the distance around, about 6,91 metres, times the height. Add the lid circle. About 14,17 square metres of skin. One litre covers 8, so you need 1,77 litres — and here's the rule that saves your Sunday: shopping ALWAYS rounds up. Buy two. Round down and the job dies half painted with the hardware store closed. Volume fills. Area wraps. Halve the diameter. Round the shopping up.
visual_style: A cylindrical tank filling with glowing litre cubes that count up to 5 703; the curved wall peeling off like a tin label and flattening into a rectangle; a paint tin stamped 1,77 rolling up to 2; the wrong four-times-too-big tank ballooning and popping.
mood: Practical and confident, the voice of someone who checks the brochure with a calculator before paying.
pacing: Steady through the radius trap, brisk through the volume count, a grin on the supplier verdict, firm and slow on the round-up rule.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and measure anything the world sells you.
